content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's identification — the new name is the renewed covenant, known/kept only by its receiver — explains the specific content of every cited text better than the common 'new God-given identity/transformation' reading. Isaiah 62 does not merely announce a status change; it names the name: Hephzibah ('my delight is in her') and Beulah ('married'), with the LORD as bridegroom and Zion as bride (62:4-5). The content of the new name, where Scripture itself supplies it, is a marriage covenant, not a transformed personal nature. Genesis 32:28 gives the name Israel inside a covenant encounter and states its meaning as standing with God ('power with God... hast prevailed'). Isaiah 65:15 is covenant supersession: the old name left as a curse, God's servants called by another name. The book's reading of Revelation 2:17's clause 'which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it' rests on a demonstrated biblical idiom: chapter 6 establishes from Genesis 4:1 (knowing as marital union), Hosea 2:20 ('I will betroth thee... and thou shalt know the LORD'), Amos 3:2, Jeremiah 22:16, and 1 John 2:3-4 that 'knowing' in covenant contexts is relationship proved by keeping, not information held. On that idiom, 'no man knoweth the name save the receiver' means precisely what the entry says: the covenant is held — kept — only by the one to whom it is given, which is exactly what a marriage-name like Beulah would demand. The common reading treats the secrecy clause as private information or intimate uniqueness, which is coherent but leaves the marital name-contents of Isaiah 62 and the choice of the verb 'knoweth' unexplained mechanics, whereas the book derives both from prior Scripture by its stated uniform-symbol method. No counter-reading explains a supplied text that the book's core cannot explain.","book_core_identification":"The 'new name' symbolizes the renewed covenant itself — the covenant relationship (pictured as marriage) that God confers — rather than a transformed personal identity or a private token; the clause 'no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it' means the covenant is known in the biblical sense (held/kept in relationship) only by its recipient.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The gloss 'known — kept': reading 'knoweth' in Revelation 2:17 through the covenantal idiom of knowing established in chapter 6 (Gen 4:1; Hos 2:20; Amos 3:2; Jer 22:16; 1 John 2:3-4)","The adjective 'renewed', anchored in the restoration context of Isaiah 62 and the name-transfer of Isaiah 65:15","The cross-link to the sheep/voice/name cluster of John 10 and the forthcoming 'Name' chapter"],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream reading: the new name symbolizes the new, God-given identity, character, and status of the redeemed person — the old identity replaced by a divinely conferred one — with the secrecy of Revelation 2:17 signifying the unique, intimate personal relationship between the individual believer and Christ (or, in a variant, the name is Christ's/God's own name placed on the believer as a mark of ownership, per Rev 3:12; 14:1; 22:4).","counter_core_identification":"The new name is a divinely bestowed new identity/status of the transformed person, with the 'no man knoweth' clause denoting private, individual intimacy or the hiddenness of the name's content.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"To materially contradict the book, the counter must hold that the name signifies the person's transformed nature/identity as such, and that 'knoweth' in Revelation 2:17 denotes informational secrecy or private intimacy, such that the name is not the covenant relationship itself and the secrecy clause is not about exclusive covenant-keeping.","counter_case":["Renaming narratives (Abram/Abraham, Jacob/Israel, Simon/Peter) accompany a change in the person's role and character, supporting 'new identity'","Revelation 2:17's emphasis that no one else knows the name naturally reads as a secret, personal possession — a devotional intimacy reading with long pedigree (Spurgeon, MacDonald)","Revelation 3:12 has Christ writing God's name, the New Jerusalem's name, and 'my new name' on the overcomer, suggesting the name marks ownership and belonging rather than being 'the covenant' itself","Isaiah 62:2-4 can be read as vindication and changed status of Zion (from 'Forsaken' to 'Delighted-in'), i.e., status change, without needing the name to be the covenant"],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Isaiah 62:4-5 supplies the actual content of the new name — Hephzibah and Beulah, 'married' — and immediately expounds it as a bridegroom-bride covenant; the book's identification predicts exactly this marital content, while 'new identity' merely accommodates it","The verb choice in Revelation 2:17 ('knoweth', not 'seeth' or 'possesseth') is derived from the demonstrated covenantal idiom of knowing (Gen 4:1; Hos 2:20; Amos 3:2; Jer 22:16), explaining why exclusive knowing marks the receiver — one is either in the covenant or not","Genesis 32:28 and Isaiah 65:15 both situate renaming inside covenant transactions (prevailing with God; the old name becoming a curse as servants are called by another name), unifying all four cited texts under one symbol per the book's stated cross-canon method","The reading integrates with the adjacent John 10 cluster (sheep know the Shepherd's voice, He calls his own by name, strangers are not known), where knowing is covenant membership, not private information"],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["The intimacy reading gives a simple, surface-level account of 'which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it' without requiring the covenantal-knowing idiom","The ownership variant (Rev 3:12; 14:1; 22:4) explains the parallel foreheads/name texts of Revelation that the book's printed entry does not cite or address","Historical-critical background (tessera, acquittal pebble) offers an explanation of the white stone itself, which the book's entry leaves untreated"],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Isaiah 62:2-5 — the new name is expressly Hephzibah/Beulah, i.e., a marriage-covenant name, with the bridegroom-bride exposition attached","Genesis 4:1; Hosea 2:20; Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 22:16; 1 John 2:3-4 — the chapter-6 derivation that biblical 'knowing' is covenant relationship proved by keeping, which converts Revelation 2:17's secrecy clause into exclusive covenant possession","Isaiah 65:15 — the old name left as a curse while God's servants are called by another name, a covenant transfer, not a mere character change","Genesis 32:28 — Israel conferred inside a covenant encounter with a covenantal etymology ('power with God... prevailed')"],"unresolved_objections":["The white stone of Revelation 2:17 is not explained by the entry; background readings (tessera/admission token) address it and the book does not","Revelation 3:12's triple name (God's name, New Jerusalem, Christ's 'my new name') is not treated; the ownership/belonging variant handles those parallel texts more directly","The devotional intimacy reading of 'no man knoweth' remains a possible surface reading of the clause, though it does not account for the marital name-content of Isaiah 62 or the covenantal knowing idiom","'Renewed' (as opposed to simply 'new') covenant rests on the restoration setting of Isaiah 62/65 rather than an explicit textual statement"],"confidence":"medium"}
